entities.name: Orbital solar supply as a reason for orbital compute
entities.note: Argument for orbital compute. The pack records who states the proposition and when, not whether it is true.

proposition.criterion: Solar power in suitable orbits is more continuous or more abundant than on Earth, and this is given as a reason to place computing there.

entities.name: Radiative cooling in orbit as an advantage
entities.note: Argument for orbital compute. The pack records who states the proposition and when, not whether it is true.

proposition.criterion: Rejecting heat by radiation to space lets an orbital data centre avoid the water use, chillers or cooling energy of terrestrial data centres.

entities.name: Terrestrial constraints as a reason to move compute off Earth
entities.note: Argument for orbital compute. The pack records who states the proposition and when, not whether it is true.

proposition.criterion: Constraints on building or powering data centres on Earth (land, permitting, grid connection, power supply, water or local impact) limit their growth, and placing compute in orbit is said to avoid them.

entities.name: Falling launch prices as the condition of viability
entities.note: Argument for orbital compute, conditional in form. The pack records who states the proposition and when, not whether it is true.

proposition.criterion: The economic viability of orbital compute depends on launch prices falling, stated with or without a price threshold per kilogram.

entities.name: Lower lifecycle emissions of orbital data centres
entities.note: Argument for orbital compute. The pack records who states the proposition and when, not whether it is true.

proposition.criterion: Orbital data centres can have lower lifecycle greenhouse-gas emissions than terrestrial ones, with or without stated conditions (such as a less emissive launcher).

entities.name: Heat rejection in orbit as a limit
entities.note: Limiting or contesting argument. The pack records who states the proposition and when, not whether it is true.

proposition.criterion: Because heat in orbit can be rejected only by radiation, thermal management (for example the required radiator area) is a significant engineering or cost constraint on orbital compute.

entities.name: Radiation effects on computing hardware in orbit
entities.note: Limiting argument. The pack records who states the proposition and when, not whether it is true.

proposition.criterion: Ionizing radiation in orbit degrades or disrupts computing hardware, requiring shielding, redundancy, error correction or hardened parts.

entities.name: No in-place maintenance or repair
entities.note: Limiting argument. The pack records who states the proposition and when, not whether it is true.

proposition.criterion: Failed hardware in orbit cannot practically be repaired or replaced by technicians as on Earth, so failures must be met by redundancy, module replacement or launches.

entities.name: Launch and build costs still too high
entities.note: Contesting argument. The pack records who states the proposition and when, not whether it is true.

proposition.criterion: At current or assumed launch and spacecraft prices, computing in orbit costs more than equivalent computing on Earth.

entities.name: Bandwidth and latency to the ground as a limit
entities.note: Limiting argument. The pack records who states the proposition and when, not whether it is true.

proposition.criterion: Links between orbital compute and users or data on the ground (bandwidth, latency, ground stations) limit which workloads orbital compute can serve.

entities.name: Harm to astronomy, the night sky or the orbital environment
entities.note: Contesting argument. The pack records who states the proposition and when, not whether it is true.

proposition.criterion: Large orbital-data-centre constellations would harm astronomical observation or the night sky, or raise collision, debris or atmospheric risks.

object.value: 5-gigawatt orbital data centre with solar and cooling panels about 4 km by 4 km

claims.subject: turyshev-odc-2026

claims.subject: lumen-orbit-wp-2024
claims.statement: The Lumen Orbit white paper (September 2024) argues that, if best practices are followed, terrestrial astronomy is unlikely to be affected by orbital data centres in its chosen dawn-dusk orbit, while naming debris mitigation as a key hurdle.
claims.qualification: A proponent's view of the issue, earlier than the critical texts located.

evidence.passage: if best practices are followed15 then the terrestrial astronomy community is unlikely to be impacted by orbital data centers in our selected orbit

claims.subject: lincei-fcc-comment-2026
claims.statement: The Accademia dei Lincei's FCC comment (March 2026) expresses grave concern about SpaceX's proposed orbital data centres, arguing that they would very negatively affect ground-based optical astronomy and raise collision and debris risks.
claims.qualification: Earliest located among the texts retrieved for this strand on 2026-10-28 (company, agency, scientific-society and arXiv texts on orbital compute, 2019-2026, found by web discovery searches and direct retrieval); not a claim that no earlier text exists. Addresses the SpaceX application, though it says its considerations have general validity. The AAS petition on the same application was not retrievable (aas.org refused).

evidence.passage: Expresses grave concern about the proposed Orbital Data Centers (ODCs).
the ODC satellites would very negatively affect astronomical optical observations on the ground
Paraphrase: the comment emphasises the risk of accidental collisions or failures of the autonomous avoidance system, which would create an uncontrolled number of space debris.

claims.subject: marcy-odc-2026
claims.statement: Marcy's preprint (March 2026) argues that kilometre-scale orbital computing arrays would alter the night and daytime sky and increase the likelihood of collisions that could trigger runaway debris production.
claims.qualification: Preprint submitted to MNRAS Letters; its brightness figures are modelled. It calls the concept technically attractive while raising these concerns.

evidence.passage: such kilometre-scale structures at roughly 500 km altitude would dramatically alter both the night and daytime sky
while increasing the likelihood of collisions that could trigger runaway debris production
These orbiting computing facilities therefore pose serious astronomical, technical, and cultural concerns.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 1, abstract and title block
evidence.passage: Paraphrase: the preprint is marked as submitted to Letters of the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society and calls the concept technically attractive.

claims.subject: swf-odc-filings-post-2026
claims.statement: Secure World Foundation stated (May 2026) that orbital data-centre applications by SpaceX, Starcloud and Blue Origin should not be treated as routine licensing matters and asked the FCC to require system-level analysis of cumulative collision risks.
claims.qualification: Context: asks for scrutiny and phased authorisation, and says it is not arguing against innovation; the filings themselves were not read.

evidence.passage: these applications should not be treated as routine satellite licensing matters
cumulative collision risks, post-mission disposal performance, and aggregate interference effects
Paraphrase: SWF says its filings are not arguments against innovation but for regulatory oversight.

openQuestions.question: Do the orbital arguments (OC1-OC11) belong in the thought spine (propositions) or the governance spine?
openQuestions.recommended: Thought spine, as propositions with document subjects and earliest-located roles, as the scope already proposes: they are arguments made in papers, white papers and letters, and the propositions model exists for them. The governance spine (Frontier AI governance) should hold the regulatory records - the FCC applications, acceptances and the Lincei and Secure World Foundation submissions - and link to the propositions those submissions argue. Two records carry both roles (the Lincei comment and the SWF post); keep them as argument records here and cross-link from governance rather than duplicate.

openQuestions.question: Proposed predicates beyond the shared list: operation_stated (organisation -> infrastructure: an operator states a spacecraft carrying compute is operating or has run a stated workload) and accepted_for_filing (public_body -> document: a regulator accepts an application for filing).
openQuestions.recommended: Adopt operation_stated as the spacecraft analogue of site_status_stated, or merge both into one status predicate with a subject-type rule; adopt accepted_for_filing, because acceptance is a procedural step that must not be read as approval (the record now uses time.basis 'approval' for want of a 'procedural' basis - consider adding one).
